entry.title: Mega Pinball Fantasies - Pinball Fantasies comes to the Sega Mega Drive via DavidGames
entry.content:
It's been some time since we've featured any Pinball news, so to change all that, here's Mega Pinball Fantasies for the Sega Mega Drive. Originally released in 1992 by Digital Illusions, the iconic title has been recreated for the SEGA Mega Drive under the name Mega Pinball Fantasies. Developed by DavidGames, this ambitious 16-bit port began as a passionate personal project during the pandemic lockdown. After years of research and development, the project aims to recreate the experience of this legendary video game on the hardware of our beloved 16-bit console.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The release faithfully features all four of the original, distinctly themed tables. Players can chase high scores across the vibrant amusement park atmosphere of Party Land, test their reflexes with the high-octane racing elements of Speed Devils, compete for massive virtual cash prizes in Billion Dollar Gameshow, or brave the eerie, supernatural horrors of Stones 'N Bones. More than just a simple conversion, this upcoming port serves as a technical tribute to the capabilities of the Mega Drive, offering Mega Drive owners a brand-new way to experience this masterful pinball simulator by Digital Illusions.

entry.title: Death Mask 3D - Apache Software Amiga FPS using using a first-person 3D engine
entry.content:
CodyJarrett has made available another update for Death Mask 3D, a technical overhaul of Apache Software’s classic Amiga title. While the original game relied on a grid-based, step-by-step movement style reminiscent of Dungeon Master, this updated iteration transforms the experience into a true first-person shooter akin to Wolfenstein 3D. Built with the assistance of the Claude AI model, the new project renders all 34 original campaign missions and 10 multiplayer arenas in a fluid, continuous 3D engine. It preserves the authentic atmosphere of the source material by retaining the original wall textures, enemy sprites, weapon graphics, HUD layout, and sound design. Amiga owners dive into the full single-player campaign—complete with its authentic mission briefings, passwords, and cinematic intro and ending screens—or jump into split-screen mode for two-player co-op or deathmatch battles.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Latest source has a newer version

Developed for any Amiga 1200 or above, the game moves away from the original title's support for older A500 machines, requiring at least a 68020 processor, Kickstart 3.0, and 2MB of Chip RAM. Interestingly, advanced AGA chipsets are not necessary, as the visual presentation uses a 32-colour palette with the copper coprocessor handling the vibrant sky, floor, and lighting gradients. CodyJarrett has packed the release with quality-of-life enhancements, including optional Fast RAM optimization for a smoother frame rate, a native Workbench icon, and a live HUD automap that toggles with the press of a key. To ensure the game runs smoothly across different hardware configurations, players can choose between three distinct graphical detail levels or use CD32 joypad support to map strafing to the shoulder buttons. For those who simply wish to explore the nostalgic environments without the pressure of combat, built-in cheat keys are also included.

entry.content:
MrDig has announced via EAB a new project called Ultracore AGA, a work-in-progress port of the classic run-and-gun shooter. The game has a bit of a history. It originally started development for the Amiga by Digital Illusions under the name Hardcore but was sadly cancelled before completion. Decades later via Strictly Limited Games, the project was resurrected and officially released for modern platforms like the Sega Mega Drive, PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch under the title Ultracore. Now, inspired by community discussions on the English Amiga Board (EAB), MrDig has taken on the challenge of bringing this action-packed title back to its original roots.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The early progress on the port looks promising. A newly released gameplay video showcases the title screen and attract mode, leading into actual gameplay with full sound effects and streaming audio. The current "Ultracore+" build runs at stock Amiga 1200 speeds, though it currently requires a hefty 30 megabytes of Fast RAM to stream the uncompressed, 8-bit mono music. MrDig considers the project a work in progress but has ambitions for the final version. The ultimate goal is to optimize the game so that it runs smoothly with full sound and music on a standard, stock A1200 equipped with only a modest amount of Fast RAM.

entry.title: Sword - A Polish Amiga Classic That Deserved Better (Amigaguru Guest Review)
entry.content:
Sword, developed by Serio Comic, was their second (and possibly final) game, and it clearly showed how much they had learned since their debut game Gate 2 Freedom which was also a platformer. The game delivers plenty of replay value, backed by a consistent visual style and cohesive level design throughout. Every stage introduces enough new ideas and challenges to keep you coming back for more.

One feature that initially annoyed me was the strict time limit, but it also introduced something I've never seen before or since. When you die, you restart at the beginning of the level, but every enemy you've killed and every item you've collected remains gone. Even better, the timer is frozen until you reach the point where you originally died. This removes much of the frustration usually associated with retracing your steps, and because you already know where many of the traps and tricky jumps are, progression still feels natural even after repeated deaths.

A Challenge, Lots Of Bosses, A Timer And A Gun...

Sword throws plenty of challenges your way, yet your only means of defence is a fairly weak gun with one of the strangest sound effects I've ever heard in a game. You get used to it over time, but I still wish there had been weapon upgrades or additional health boosts to make combat a little more rewarding.

The levels vary considerably in both length and difficulty. Some can feel quite drawn out because your weapon is so weak, forcing you to spend a lot of time clearing enemies and obstacles. There are also a few light puzzle elements scattered throughout the game, but thankfully they never disrupt the pacing. As most of my readers know by now, I generally dislike puzzles in platform and action games, yet Sword never pushed me to that breaking point. In fact, I've completed it at least three times over the last three decades. Sword is far from a new game; it originally launched in 1998 and was one of the final commercial releases for the Amiga 500 before receiving a revival many years later.

One of the aspects that impressed me at launch, and still does today, is just how technically accomplished the game is. There's plenty of parallax scrolling, huge bosses, fantastic music and sound effects running simultaneously, responsive controls, and excellent pacing across a large variety of levels and locations. The game even includes an auto-scrolling snowboarding bonus stage, something you almost never saw on the Amiga at the time. While the main character sprite isn't particularly remarkable, it's important to remember that this is an Amiga 500 title requiring just 1MB of RAM and spread across four floppy disks. Considering those limitations, Sword makes outstanding use of the hardware and puts many older, and even some newer, Amiga games to shame.


This One Fell Between Two Worlds...

This was also the last title from Titan Computer published for the classic Amiga OCS/ECS hardware. Afterwards, the company published several ground breaking PowerPC releases for the platform, including Shogoand Heretic II (which I worked on for Hyperion, by the way). That makes Sword something of a swansong for the ECS and AGA era. There were several ambitious projects planned afterwards, such as Evil's Doom and Alien Nations, but unfortunately most of them disappeared into development hell and never saw release.

Sword sold poorly, likely due to a combination of being a Polish production and receiving a very limited print run. As a result, boxed copies are now considered quite rare, even if that rarity isn't reflected on sites such as Hall of Light or Lemon Amiga. Of course, it didn't help that the game arrived during the height of the original PlayStation era, when flashy 3D games dominated the market. Back then, many of us wanted the Amiga to follow the same path rather than continue producing what looked like "simple" 2D games.

Ironically, looking back today, it's the 2D titles that have aged gracefully. Most early 3D games now look rough at best, while quality pixel art remains as appealing as ever. Sword still looks fantastic today, just like other great 2D classics from the era such as The Misadventures of Lomax and Hercules on the PlayStation.

The Box & The Stuff Inside...

Sword - The Breathtaking Game (as it says on the floppy labels) might not come with the most impressive packaging or packed-in extras, but it certainly features some of the most unusual box art of its era. Not my favourite at launch, but the artwork gradually grew on me over the following decade. I did take photos of the back of the box, but they didn't turn out particularly well due to just how much information (and the amount of color crash/mix) is crammed onto it. If you're interested in seeing it, I can always take another shot, but for now you can simply head over to Hall of Light and check out my box scan there.

The included manual is printed entirely in black and white, and the floppy disk labels follow the same budget-friendly approach. Considering the state of the Amiga market at the time, that's perfectly understandable. Amiga games were struggling commercially, and publishers were understandably reluctant to spend heavily on packaging and presentation for products that might never sell enough copies to justify the investment.

Summary...

A really solid game that was overlooked and forgotten by many Amiga fans. Had it been released six years earlier, it could easily have been a major hit because all the ingredients for success are here. That's exactly why I've added it to my long-running TGWNTABS series, which now stands at a whopping 24 articles dedicated to games that you absolutely need to play before deciding that only modern games are worth your time.

Whatever way you get hold of it, do yourself a favour and give Sword a try. It remains one of the finest late-era Amiga platform shooters, and it deserves far more recognition than it ever received. If you enjoy it, spread the word, leave a comment online, and help ensure this forgotten classic continues to shine.

As mentioned, Sword is a fairly rare Commodore Amiga 500 release, meaning you'll most likely need to track it down through abandonware archives or other preservation sources. Finding a boxed copy today is incredibly difficult, although with more and more collectors selling off their collections these days, you never know. It's a little sad to see, if I'm being honest. 

Guest article by AmigaGuru

entry.title: The Rescue - A new action game for the C64 by Fernando64JJ
entry.content:
Here's a non AI game for you to enjoy and it's Fernando64JJ's latest C64 game 'The Rescue'. In this game, you are transported back to 1987 inside a perilous jungle territory ruled by the ruthless Colonel Varga. The story follows protagonist John Jericho on a high-stakes mission to save Adri, a medical camp worker who was abducted after documenting the militia's atrocities. Players must navigate two intense helicopter flight phases across coastlines and deltas, dodging enemy jets and gunships, before transitioning into a gruelling ten-stage ground assault that spans enemy airstrips, ancient temples, and Varga's heavily fortified compound.

The game features full-screen title artwork, distinct illustrations for each level, and a cinematic SID soundtrack composed by Retroverse Jack. entry.title: Icy Escort - A route-planning Platformer released by Donut 80 for the C64
entry.content:
Welcome to the latest game called Icy Escort, a brand-new Commodore 64 title developed by Donut 80. In this charming puzzle-platformer, players guide a dedicated mother penguin on a race against time to gather her missing chicks before the clock strikes midnight. Each snowy stage requires players to scout the treacherous wintry landscape to locate the lost babies. As each chick is successfully rescued, it tags along directly behind the mother, forming a growing line of penguins that follows her every move through the frozen wilderness.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The gameplay mechanics offer a twist on traditional movement by relying heavily on momentum and environmental rules. Players navigate the world using just a single jump button, while the penguin automatically marches forward. Changing direction is impossible on your own; instead, you must rely on strategic bounces off arrow indicators, crates, and the borders of the screen. This limitation transforms the platforming into an intricate puzzle where timing and careful path planning are essential to avoid hazards. Along the journey, players can stomp on enemies and collect ice cream treats to reset a multiplier timer and boost their high scores, though safely rescuing every single chick remains the ultimate goal.

According to the website description, the developer translated the original NES console code into native Motorola 68000 assembly language. The entire game fits onto a single floppy disk, making it accessible to anyone owning a classic Amiga system equipped with just 512 KB of chip RAM. Furthermore, the game natively supports both PAL and NTSC display formats. The conversion underwent an exhaustive quality control process to match the target hardware frame for frame. entry.title: Alex Kidd GX in a Miracle AI World GX – An AI Conversion project is in the works bringing the SMS classic over to the Amstrad GX4000!
entry.content:
Overange has sparked quite a stir in the Amstrad scene by bringing SEGA’s classic Alex Kidd in Miracle World to the Amstrad GX4000 under the title Alex Kidd GX. What began roughly two weeks ago as a simple experiment to see how hard it would be to convert a Master System title has quickly snowballed into working towards a full-blown port featuring all 17 original levels. Built on top of the Sonic GX engine—courtesy of NoRecess464 and the Condense team—the game isn't running through clunky emulation, but is instead being rewritten from the ground up in native Z80 assembly to work within the GX4000's specific hardware and memory bank limits.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The real twist behind this rapid progress, however, is how the code is actually being written. Overange has been completely upfront about relying heavily on artificial intelligence to do the programming grunt work. Using ChatGPT to help brainstorm tasks and draft instructions, the developer hands the heavy lifting over to Anthropic’s Claude to generate the game code. Overange acts as the quality assurance tester, running the builds on both the WinAPE emulator and real GX4000 hardware via PicoCart and Flash cartridges, then feeding screenshots, video clips, and bug reports back to the AI to refine the game.

While using AI to write code is nothing new, Overange recently experienced a jaw-dropping moment that showed just how autonomous these tools have become. After reporting a glitch, Claude requested direct access to the developer's PC to investigate the issue firsthand. Without being told which drive or folder the software was hidden in, the AI took control of the mouse cursor, tracked down the WinAPE emulator on its own, booted up the ROM, and literally played through the tricky section of the game to recreate the bug. It is a slightly eerie yet fascinating glimpse into the future of retro development, proving that human creativity paired with machine autonomy can change the way we think of game development in this modern age.

entry.title: The Abbey of Crime (Amiga 500 Version) - A tribute port of the 1987 game by Paco Menéndez and Juan Delcán
entry.content:
Here's some nostalgia for you 8biters! As developer vnomis has released a faithful port of the 1987 Spanish classic The Abbey of Crime. Originally created by Paco Menéndez and Juan Delcán for Opera Soft, this isometric murder mystery puts you in the robes of Friar William alongside your young novice, Adso. You have just seven days to uncover who is behind a string of sinister deaths inside a secluded monastery, all while sticking strictly to the Abbot's rigid schedule of daily meals and prayers so you don't get thrown out before solving the case.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Designed to run straight from a single self-booting floppy disk on a standard PAL Amiga 500 with 512 KB of RAM, this release keeps the original game's logic intact while introducing some quality-of-life upgrades. Players can toggle between English and Spanish text, enjoy original or enhanced audio, and pick from three distinct visual styles—including the classic Amstrad CPC palette, an enhanced look, and a Film mode. To make the famously unforgiving adventure a bit more accessible too, vnomis even added direct directional controls alongside the original tank-style movement, on-disk save slots, and dedicated object and mirror screens to cut down on keyboard reliance. There is even a handy bot to handle your daily routines between canonical hours, plus a self-playing movie mode that solves the entire mystery automatically unless you decide to jump in and take over.

entry.title: Kung-Fu Master A500 Edition - A port of the 1984 Kung-Fu Master Arcade game to Amiga OCS

Modern Vintage Gamer has released a brand-new homebrew port of Irem’s 1984 scrolling beat-'em-up classic, Kung-Fu Master for the Commodore Amiga OCS chipset. Titled Kung-Fu Master A500 Edition, this release delivers a near-identical 1:1 recreation of the original arcade hit, complete with all of the classic sound effects and music. Remarkably according to the developer, the game runs at a silky-smooth 50 or 60 frames per second even on stock Amiga 500 hardware, while also taking advantage of Fast RAM detection and automatic NTSC switching. Players can customize their experience through a dedicated options menu that lets you tweak difficulty settings, select your starting round, toggle auto-fire or invincibility, and choose between keyboard, single-button, or two-button controls—all while keeping track of your best runs with built-in high score saving.

To save her, you will have to fight your way up through five distinct floors packed with relentless waves of grippers, knife throwers, dragons, snakes, and exploding balls. Surviving the gauntlet requires defeating the tough guardian waiting at the end of each level before you can climb the stairs to the next challenge.

Originally written by Bob Polin for the Atari 400 and 800, the game later received a popular Commodore 64 conversion by Peter Adams, though it famously skipped the Amiga entirely until now. For the initial release however, the port will stick closely to the original Atari 8x8 tiles and sprites rather than the flashier Commodore 64 graphics, largely because the Atari source code is readily available and arguably boasts superior audio. However, fans can look forward to an Amiga Enhanced version with upgraded visuals further down the road.

entry.title: Maniac Mansion Deluxe AGA - Check out the latest AGA remake of the original Lucasfilm Game Adventure for the Amiga!
entry.content:
Classic adventure fans here's something you may be interested in, as developer Tecniman has just released the final version 2.0 of Maniac Mansion Deluxe AGA. This impressive release brings the beloved PC version of Lucasfilm Games classic natively to the Amiga platform as an AGA remake. Built around the assets and scripts from the original PC installer, Tecniman wrote a completely new game engine from the ground up to recreate all the rooms, puzzles, cutscenes, and character behaviours. While AI tools lent a helping hand in analysing the original game and assisting with code reviews, getting everything running smoothly required massive amounts of manual testing, bug fixing, and careful comparison against the source material.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Getting such a visually rich game onto classic hardware was no small feat, especially since the primary target is a stock Amiga 1200 equipped with a 68020 processor and AGA graphics. To squeeze all those colourful backgrounds and object masks into the machine's tight 2 MB of Chip RAM, the custom engine dynamically dumps each room's data from memory upon exit before loading the next. The developer also had to overcome tricky technical hurdles like rendering characters behind foreground scenery and perfecting screen transitions, while handing audio duties over to ptplayer to drive music modules and sound effects straight through the Paula chip. The port has been thoroughly put through its paces on real hardware including an Amiga CD32 with a hard drive, an accelerated A1200 with a 68030, a PiStorm setup, and a Vampire V4.

Players delving into this new 2.0 version can expect 36 playable rooms, 41 scene sequences, 67 inventory items, 18 music tracks, 87 sound effects, and four intro clips. Alongside this is a brand-new intro screen and localised graphics while the final update squashes lingering visual bugs involving the fence, the TV advert, and the dungeon graffiti. Getting started is as simple as copying the game folder over to Workbench without altering the Data directory, where players can launch the streamlined standard executable—now roughly half the size of the included bug-logging Test edition—while Vampire V4 owners can easily toggle the CPUFAST ToolType to YES if they spot any mask flickering.

entry.title: Xenon 2 Megablast - A never released speccy game has been unofficially ported to the ZX Spectrum 128K
entry.content:
Thirty plus years after its original cancellation, the Bitmap Brothers’ legendary shoot-'em-up Xenon 2 Megablast may have just landed on the ZX Spectrum 128K courtesy of developer Outsoftware. A game that many thought would never see the light of day on Sinclair's classic 8-bit machine. The story behind this long-lost port stretches all the way back to 1991, when Commodore 64 coder and musician Dave Spicer put together an ambitious technical demo to pitch a Spectrum version of the game. Featuring sleek, minimalist early graphics by Jason Brashill, the full-screen demo ran at an impressive 25 frames per second and looked remarkable for the hardware. Despite the promising showcase, publisher Mirrorsoft had little interest in backing 8-bit conversions at the time and ultimately rejected the pitch.

Determined not to give up right away, Spicer later upgraded his demo with parallax scrolling to better rival the 16-bit editions, trading off just a touch of speed in the process. His plan was to send both the fast standard build and the newer parallax version over to Your Sinclair magazine, hoping that press coverage and fan excitement might force Mirrorsoft to change its mind. That publicity push never materialised and the project was quietly shelved, making Outsoftware’s brand-new release a thrilling piece of gaming history that may be worth loading up on your ZX Spectrum or ZX Next 3!

Massive thanks to Gamesthatwerent for the history of the lost game and elmundodelspectrum's news about the latest conversion.
